Yeovil.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Somerset
s1loc: Yeovil anchors its visitor appeal on the Fleet Air Arm Museum at nearby Yeovilton, home to Europe's largest collection of naval aircraft, where visitors walk through Concorde 002, board a recreated aircraft carrier flight deck and explore a Search and Rescue Sea King helicopter. The Yeovil Railway Centre adds steam-age heritage with restored locomotives and a turntable, making the pair the marquee draw for visitors heading into south Somerset.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Yeovil Country Park and the tranquil Ninesprings valley, where wooded trails, lakes, hidden sculptures and picnic lawns spread across the heart of town. The wider park network links walking and cycling routes out into the rolling hills, and Yeovil Recreation Centre and the surrounding green spaces give family and activity operators a steady seasonal draw across the warmer months and beyond.

Heritage and culture run through the Elizabethan Montacute House, a National Trust mansion of golden Ham stone with grand gardens and a long gallery just outside town, and the town's glove-making past gives Yeovil Town the nickname the Glovers. The Octagon Theatre, now undergoing a major creative-arts revamp, the Community Heritage Access Centre and a busy events calendar give guides and cultural operators plenty of local material.

The visitor trade draws on town-centre and country hotels and guest houses, with guides working the aviation heritage, Montacute and the Ham Hill country park. Yeovil Junction and Pen Mill stations link to London Waterloo and Bristol, while Huish Park is home to Yeovil Town for home games, and the surrounding draws of Dorchester, Bridgwater and Taunton feed a steady seasonal flow into south Somerset.

Welwyn Garden City.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of garden-city Hertfordshire
s1loc: Welwyn Garden City was founded by Sir Ebenezer Howard in 1920 as the second of Britain's garden cities, and its tree-lined Parkway, the Campus and the broad Howardsgate boulevard remain the marquee draw for visitors exploring planned-town heritage. The nearby Welwyn Roman Baths, the preserved remains of the third-century Dicket Mead villa housed in a steel vault beneath the A1(M), give visitors an unusual Roman landmark on the town's doorstep.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Stanborough Park, a 126-acre countryside retreat with two lakes for sailing, paddleboarding and fishing, plus walking trails, a children's play area and the Stanborough activity centre. The wider Lemsford and Mimram valley footpaths, parkland greens and the open spaces threaded through the garden-city design give family and activity operators a steady seasonal draw across the year.

Heritage and culture run through Mill Green Museum and Mill, a working water-powered flour mill with galleries of local history and Roman finds, and the Hatfield House estate close by, the Jacobean former home of Queen Elizabeth I with its 40-acre gardens and major outdoor events such as Battle Proms and Folk by the Oak. The Howard Centre and a calendar of garden-city festivals fill out the local scene.

The visitor trade draws on town and roadside hotels and guest houses, with guides leading garden-city, Roman baths and Hatfield House tours. Welwyn Garden City station on the East Coast Main Line links fast to London King's Cross, and easy reach of the A1(M) carries day-trippers in, while the surrounding draws of Hatfield, Stevenage and Hertford feed a steady seasonal flow into Hertfordshire.

Carlton.region: Carlton and the borough of Gedling
Carlton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Gedling and the Trent valley
s1loc: Carlton sits in the borough of Gedling on Nottingham's eastern edge, and its marquee draw is Gedling Country Park, 580 acres of footpaths, grassland and wildlife laid out on the former Gedling Colliery site since 2015, with sweeping views across the Trent valley. A rustic mining-tower slide, the colliery memorial garden and Cafe 1899 mark the park's pit heritage and make it the standout visitor site close to town.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across Carlton's parks and recreation grounds and out to the colour-coded walking and cycling routes of Gedling Country Park, with its play areas, lagoons for duck feeding and open grasslands. Burton Joyce and the Trent-side meadows beyond give family and activity operators riverside walks and country trails, keeping the outdoor offer busy across the warmer months and into the year.

Heritage and culture run through Carlton's old framework-knitting and mining past, the medieval All Hallows church at Gedling with its tall spire, and the wider Gedling heritage of colliery and canal. The Carlton Forum and local community venues host events through the year, while the nearby Bonington Theatre at Arnold gives guides and cultural operators a steady programme close at hand.

The visitor trade draws on hotels and guest houses across the Nottingham fringe, with guides working the country park, the Trent valley and the city beyond. Frequent buses and the Netherfield railway station link Carlton into Nottingham's transport network, and easy reach of the city centre carries day-trippers in, while the surrounding draws of Arnold, Nottingham and West Bridgford feed a steady seasonal flow. Colwick Country Park, Colwick Hall and Nottingham Racecourse lie just across the Trent, adding to the local draw.

West Bridgford.region: West Bridgford and the Trent valley
West Bridgford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Trent-side sporting belt
s1loc: West Bridgford carries two of the most famous names in British sport across the River Trent from Nottingham. Trent Bridge, the third-oldest Test venue and headquarters of Nottinghamshire County Cricket Club, regularly hosts England internationals beneath its grand Victorian pavilion, while the City Ground, home of Nottingham Forest, stands half a mile away on the riverbank, making the sporting belt the marquee draw for visitors to the town.

The leisure and activity layer is led by the Holme Pierrepont National Water Sports Centre, 270 acres of country park with a 2km regatta lake and a white-water rafting course just east of town. Rushcliffe Country Park near Ruddington, the riverside meadows of Lady Bay and the green expanse of Bridgford Park give family and activity operators a varied seasonal draw across the year.

Heritage and culture run through the bustling Central Avenue with its bars, cafes and independent shops, the riverside promenade by Trent Bridge and the suburban character of Lady Bay between the river and the disused Grantham Canal. Test and one-day cricket fixtures, Forest home games and a busy calendar of events along the Trent give guides and cultural operators a strong sporting and riverside narrative.

The visitor trade draws on hotels and guest houses across the riverside and into Nottingham, with guides working Trent Bridge tours, the watersports centre and the city beyond. West Bridgford lies a couple of miles from Nottingham station and the tram network, with easy reach of the city centre carrying day-trippers in, while the surrounding draws of Nottingham, Beeston and Carlton feed a steady seasonal flow.

Beckenham.region: Beckenham and the borough of Bromley
Beckenham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south-east London's leafy suburbs
s1loc: Beckenham anchors its visitor appeal on Beckenham Place Park, the largest green space in the borough of Lewisham at 98 hectares, where the Grade II-listed Palladian mansion built for John Cator now serves as a community hub and cafe. The park's restored Georgian lake, the first purpose-built open-water swimming venue of its kind in London, draws swimmers and boaters through the year and makes the estate the marquee local draw.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across Kelsey Park, with its boating lakes, aviaries and formal gardens, and Beckenham Place Park's BMX and skate park, nature trails, cycle routes and parkrun. The wooded walks, playgrounds and lakeside picnic lawns across both parks, with Crystal Palace Park a short way north, give family and activity operators a steady seasonal draw across the warmer months and beyond.

Heritage and culture run through the Edwardian Bowie Bandstand in Croydon Road Recreation Ground, the only surviving McCallum and Hope bandstand in the UK, where David Bowie performed at the 1969 Growth festival and which now hosts the Bowie's Beckenham Oddity celebration. The recreation ground's long history of fetes, flower shows and commemoration services gives guides and cultural operators a distinctive local story.

The visitor trade draws on hotels and guest houses across the leafy south-east London suburbs, with guides working the parks, the Bowie heritage and Crystal Palace nearby. Beckenham Junction station and the Tramlink service link quickly into central London and Croydon, carrying day-trippers in, while the surrounding draws of Bromley, Lewisham and Croydon feed a steady seasonal flow into the borough.

Sutton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the borough of Sutton
s1loc: Sutton anchors its visitor appeal on Honeywood Museum, a seventeenth-century chalk-and-flint house standing at the water's edge of Carshalton Ponds, the borough's flagship heritage house with exhibits on the Tudor palace of Nonsuch and an Edwardian billiards room. The historic buildings and water features around the ponds form one of the most picturesque corners of any London suburb and make the area the marquee draw for visitors.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Nonsuch Park, the last surviving part of Henry VIII's deer-hunting park, where open parkland, woodland walks and the Grade II-listed Nonsuch Mansion draw families and ramblers. Carshalton's lakes and gardens, the riverside walks of the River Wandle and the green spaces threaded across the borough give family and activity operators a varied seasonal draw across the year.

Heritage and culture run through the Tudor Whitehall house in Cheam, a timber-framed survivor of around 1500 with a peaceful garden and tea rooms, and the Charles Cryer Studio Theatre on Carshalton High Street. The borough's links to performers from Sir Harry Secombe to Tracey Ullman, the Nonsuch Mansion events and a calendar of local festivals give guides and cultural operators plenty of material across the seasons.

The visitor trade draws on hotels and guest houses across the Surrey-London border, with guides working Honeywood, Nonsuch Park and the Wandle heritage. Sutton, Carshalton and Cheam stations link quickly into London Victoria and London Bridge, with easy reach of the A217 carrying day-trippers in, while the surrounding draws of Croydon, Epsom and Kingston upon Thames feed a steady seasonal flow.

Banbury.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north Oxfordshire
s1loc: Banbury built its visitor appeal on the famous Banbury Cross of the nursery rhyme, the ornate 1858 monument and bronze Fine Lady statue at the meeting of the Oxford, Warwick and Shipston roads. Tooley's Boatyard beside the Oxford Canal, the oldest working dry dock in Britain repairing narrowboats since 1790 with its 200-year-old blacksmith's forge, and Banbury Museum make the canal quarter the marquee heritage draw for visitors.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Spiceball Country Park, the town's largest green space where the canal and the River Cherwell run through meadows, woodland, riverside walks, a play area and skate ramps. Canal boat trips from Tooley's, the well-paved towpath stretching out along the 78-mile Oxford Canal and the nearby countryside give family and activity operators a varied seasonal draw across the warmer months and beyond.

Heritage and culture run through the Castle Quay shopping centre on the canalside, the medieval streets and St Mary's Church at the town's core, and the annual Banbury Canal Day each October with its colourful narrowboats, music and street food. The waterway-side heritage, the Fine Lady festival traditions and a calendar of local events give guides and cultural operators a distinctive north Oxfordshire story.

The visitor trade draws on town-centre and roadside hotels and guest houses, with guides leading canal, boatyard and Banbury Cross tours. Banbury railway station on the Chiltern and Cross Country lines links to London Marylebone and Birmingham, and junction 11 of the M40 carries day-trippers in, while the surrounding draws of Bicester, Leamington Spa and Daventry feed a steady seasonal flow into north Oxfordshire.
